title: Factors affecting carcass detection at wind farms using dogs and human searchers
abstract: The use of detection dogs to effectively monitor bird and bat fatalities at wind farms is becoming increasingly popular. All studies to date agree that dogs outperform human searchers at finding bird and bat carcasses around wind turbines; however, it remains unclear how characteristics of the carcass and environmental conditions during the search may influence detection. We investigate the effect of carcass size, vegetation characteristics and weather conditions on the probability of detecting a carcass, for both dogs and humans, using data from the monitoring program of a wind farm in Spain. A generalized linear mixed model reveals a high performance of dogs ( 80% detection rate), with no clear influence of any of the variables analysed. Humans, on the contrary, were markedly affected by the size of the carcass and to some extent, by the vegetation structure. Humans performed poorly at detecting small carcasses ( 20% detection rate), more so in closed vegetation. Synthesis and applications. Our results provide evidence that dogs perform with high success rates at detecting bird and bat carcasses of different sizes under a wide range of environmental conditions. Humans, by contrast, were very poor at detecting all but the largest carcasses in open areas. We find the use of detection dogs at wind farms to be a robust and cost-effective alternative to using human searchers, most notably, when the focus is on the monitoring of fatalities of small, rare or inconspicuous species in closed vegetation.

## **Factors affecting carcass detection at wind farms using dogs and human searchers**

## **Jon Domínguez del Valle[1,2]** | **Francisco Cervantes Peralta[1,2,3]** | **María I. Jaquero Arjona[1,4]**

- 1Ideas Medioambientales S.L., Albacete, Spain

- 2Lacertida, Biodiversidad & Impacto Ambiental, Albacete, Spain

- 3Centre for Statistics in Ecology, Environment and Conservation, University of Cape Town, Cape Town, South Africa

- 4Rue Pouyer-Quertier, Fleury-sur-Andelle, France

## **Correspondence**

Jon Domínguez del Valle Email: jon.dominguez@gmail.com

**Handling Editor:** Ailsa McKenzie

## **Abstract**

1. The use of detection dogs to effectively monitor bird and bat fatalities at wind farms is becoming increasingly popular. All studies to date agree that dogs outperform human searchers at finding bird and bat carcasses around wind turbines; however, it remains unclear how characteristics of the carcass and environmental conditions during the search may influence detection.

2. We investigate the effect of carcass size, vegetation characteristics and weather conditions on the probability of detecting a carcass, for both dogs and humans, using data from the monitoring program of a wind farm in Spain.

3. A generalized linear mixed model reveals a high performance of dogs (~80% detection rate), with no clear influence of any of the variables analysed. Humans, on the contrary, were markedly affected by the size of the carcass and to some extent, by the vegetation structure. Humans performed poorly at detecting small carcasses (~20% detection rate), more so in closed vegetation.

4. _Synthesis and applications_ . Our results provide evidence that dogs perform with high success rates at detecting bird and bat carcasses of different sizes under a wide range of environmental conditions. Humans, by contrast, were very poor at detecting all but the largest carcasses in open areas. We find the use of detection dogs at wind farms to be a robust and cost-effective alternative to using human searchers, most notably, when the focus is on the monitoring of fatalities of small, rare or inconspicuous species in closed vegetation.

## **K E Y W O R D S**

bat, bird, carcass size, detection dog, environmental conditions, human searcher, mortality, wind energy

## **1** | **INTRODUCTION**

While wind energy production is mostly environmentally safe and sustainable, it raises concerns due to the mortality of birds and bats associated with wind turbines and power lines (Loss, 2016; Saidur, Rahim, Islam, & Solangi, 2011; Schuster, Bulling, & Köppel, 2015). The mortality of wildlife is particularly relevant when it affects long-lived species with low productivity and slow maturation rates, species with restricted geographical distribution or populations that

are isolated (Drewitt & Langston, 2006; Kunz et al., 2007; Kuvlesky et al., 2007; Marques et al., 2014).

In an effort to improve impact assessment, management agencies require the implementation of protocols to study wildlife mortality associated with wind farms. The common standard for quantifying fatalities consists of periodic visual carcass searches under the wind turbines (e.g. Atienza, Fierro, Infante, Valls, & Domínguez, 2011; Jenkins et al., 2015; Rodrigues et al., 2015; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 2012). However, this methodology

suffers from three main biases affecting carcass detection, and eventually, mortality estimation (Bernardino, Bispo, Costa, & Mascarenhas, 2013; Huso & Dalthorp, 2014): (a) not all carcasses remain in the field until the time of the search, (b) not all carcasses present in the field during searches are found by the observers, and (c) carcasses might fall outside of searched areas. The proportion of carcasses missed during the monitoring is estimated using experimental procedures that test the effectiveness of the search teams and the persistence of carcasses in the field. The observed proportion of missed carcasses is then included in mathematical models to correct the observed carcass counts and estimate the total number of fatalities (see Bernardino et al., 2013; Huso, Dalthorp, Miller, & Bruns, 2016). Despite estimators becoming more accurate over the years, they are necessarily bound to assumptions and limitations, and the experiments conducted to calculate correction factors (i.e. searcher efficiency and carcass persistence) are often subject to logistic and budget constraints that may lead to inaccurate estimates.

Several authors have suggested the use of trained dogs to increase carcass detection rates and minimize the impact of correction factors in mortality estimates (e.g. Reyes et al., 2016; Smallwood, Bell, & Standish, 2020). The canine olfactory system is sensitive to scents in extremely low concentrations, even when they are masked amongst complex mixtures of other scents (Beebe, Howell, & Bennett, 2016; Helton, 2009; Mackay, Smith, Long, & Parker, 2008). In addition, the historical relationship between dogs and humans and the fluent communication between the two species, make dogs an ideal asset in detection tasks (Dahlgren et al., 2011; Hurt & Smith, 2009; Mackay et al., 2008). Indeed, dogs have been used in multiple studies, involving disparate target organisms (e.g. Homan, Linz, & Peer, 2001; Long, Donovan, Mackay, Zielinski, & Buzas, 2007a, 2007b; Mackay et al., 2008; Nussear et al., 2008; Vynne et al., 2011). Studies in wind farms agree that dogs outperform human searchers; although, they also yield different, and even conflicting, interpretations of what variables influence carcass detection (Arnett, 2006; Mathews et al., 2013; Paula et al., 2011; Reyes et al., 2016; Smallwood et al., 2020).

We use data collected at a wind farm in south-east Spain to disentangle certain aspects of how environmental covariates influence carcass detection. We control for carcass size using a diverse assemblage of species of bird and bats, since previous experiences show that size is one of the main factors that facilitates carcass detection, especially for human searchers (Barrientos et al., 2018; Reyes et al., 2016; Smallwood, 2007). We characterize vegetation structure in detail, because we hypothesize that vegetation complexity could reduce detection probability, as it interferes with the formation of scent plumes (Finelli, Pentcheff, Zimmer, & Wethey, 2000) and with the visual conspicuity of the carcass (Borner et al., 2017; Eckstein, 2011), although these effects were not clear in previous studies (Arnett, 2006; Mathews et al., 2013; Paula et al., 2011). Finally, we include weatherrelated variables covering a full annual cycle, since it has been suggested that temperature and

wind conditions could affect searcher fatigue, as well as odour production and dispersion (Arnett, 2006; Mathews et al., 2013; Paula et al., 2011).

## **2** | **MATERIALS AND METHODS**

## **2.1** | **Study area**

This study was conducted at a wind farm located at the foothills of the Alcaraz Mountains in south-east Spain (38°42′N, 2°21′W). The average elevation in the region was 1,126 m a.s.l. The facility features 105 wind turbines with hub heights of 100 m and a rotor diameter of 77 m. The climate is markedly seasonal with cold, rainy winters, and hot, dry summers (Peinado, Monje, & Martínez, 2008). The vegetation corresponds to various phases of degraded calcicolous evergreen oak forest _Quercus ilex_ (Peinado et al., 2008), with small patches of Portuguese oak _Q. faginea_ , Spanish juniper _Juniperus thurifera_ and maritime pine _Pinus pinaster_ . Grazing and browsing by sheep and goats, together with timber exploitation, have sculpted the oak forests, resulting in dense Mediterranean evergreen shrub formations, with interspersed dehesas, grasslands and crops (see Appendix S1).

## **2.2** | **Detection trials**

Detection trials were conducted at 40 wind turbines selected out of the total 105 turbines of the wind farm. We aimed at having a balanced spatial coverage of the area and this selection of turbines provided a good variety of environments to conduct the detection trials. We first selected a pair of adjacent wind turbines out of all the turbines in the wind farm using a random number generator (Minitab, 2010). From these, we moved systematically along each row of turbines in a south–north direction selecting every second pair of turbines. The selection had to be slightly modified on a row by row basis to ensure an even coverage of the spatial extent of the wind farm. Centred at each wind turbine, we defined squared plots (100 m × 100 m) to conduct carcass searches (Figure 1).

We used carcasses of 50 species of birds and bats in different stages of decay (Appendix S2). We placed a random number of carcasses, between one and three, every time trials were conducted at a turbine. Carcasses were randomly allocated to a distance from the turbine between 0 and 50 m in 5 m intervals and a geographic heading (eight different headings covering 360 degrees). We selected pairs of headings and distances using a random number generator (Minitab, 2010). Carcasses were kept frozen and they were allowed time to defrost before use. The same carcass could be used in several trials unless it was suspected that it was contaminated by contact with any of the searchers (dog or human). Carcasses were always handled using plastic bags, gloves or tongs to avoid contamination with human scent.

Although both dogs and humans searched the full squared plot around the turbines, for illustration purposes, the figure is divided in two halves, showing the search pattern of dog handler on the left and the search pattern of humans on the right. The straight arrows indicate the movement of the searcher/handler, while the sinuous line approximates the movement of the dog around the handler

Trials at a turbine were considered finished when either (a) all carcasses were detected, (b) the search plot was fully covered or (c) 30 min had elapsed.

## **2.2.1** | **Trials for dogs**

We used two Belgian Malinois and one Border Collie, between 2 and 4 years of age. Training was based on positive reinforcement, using play or food to reward the dog when they displayed the desired behaviours (see Moser & McCulloch, 2010; Pryor, 2006). The basic steps in training were: (a) discriminate the scent of bird and bat carcasses, (b) search for and come into close contact with bird and bat carcasses, and (c) display an alert when in close proximity of these carcasses (sit, lie down or point). From this stage, dogs were trained to detect a wide variety of species, in different stages of decay and to follow a search pattern (see below). All dogs used in this study were previously trained in obedience and one of them in detection of missing people for search and rescue operations. In addition, FC and MJ trained and kept the dogs at home as domestic companions, which reduced logistical challenges and made training relatively fast. It took about 3 months, training between two and four times per week, to achieve a consistent performance at detecting bird and bat carcasses while following a defined search pattern.

When a dog handler team was to search at a turbine, the handler would place the selected number of carcasses at the allocated random locations. Carcasses would be thrown from a distance to avoid leaving a track on the ground that the dog could follow. To prevent the handler from giving any clues to the dog as to where the carcasses were placed, the handler always walked in a fixed search pattern during searches, at a constant pace and only communicated with the dogs to ensure they stayed within the search band. Handlers only approached and rewarded the dogs after they displayed a proper detection alert. The search pattern of the dog/handler team consisted of four parallel line transects on each search plot (Figure 1). The handler followed the transects traversing the search area, while the dog was allowed to move freely within approximately 10 m at either side of the handler. Searches were conducted perpendicular to the wind direction to maximize the probability of coming in contact with the scent cone produced by the carcasses. An average of five wind turbines were surveyed per day. Detection trials were performed weekly from 24 January 2012 to 30 July 2013, in days without precipitation or strong winds (Dahlgren et al., 2011). We conducted 589 detection trials, using 50 different species (Appendix S2).

## **2.2.2** | **Trials for humans**

For the detection trials of the human searchers, we used two individuals (alternatively) who were experienced in carcass searching at wind farms. These trials followed the same procedure as the ones for dogs, although in this case it was a helper who placed the carcasses prior to the search. Humans searched along 8–10 parallel line transects aiming to cover a 5-m wide band at each side of the transect (Figure 1). Trials for human searchers were conducted on a selection of 15 wind turbines out of the turbines searched by the dogs. Therefore, all turbines searched by humans were also searched by dogs but not the other way around. The sample of turbines searched by humans covered a similar proportion of habitats as those searched by the dogs. Humans surveyed five wind turbines per day. Fewer detection trials were conducted for human searchers than for dogs; between 16 October 2012 and 30 July 2013, on days without precipitations or strong winds, we conducted 121 detection trials using 28 different species (Appendix S2). We used the same range of carcass sizes, and in a similar proportion, for human and for dog detection trials.

## **2.3** | **Predictor variables**

We used carcass species wingspan, as a measure of carcass size. This variable is believed to play a role in carcass detection by affecting the conspicuity of the target and the volume of odour particles that it generates (Borner et al., 2017; Finelli et al., 2000; Reyes et al., 2016; Smallwood, 2007; Smallwood et al., 2020).

We also hypothesized that vegetation at ground level could interfere with the formation of scent plumes, which in turn would translate in lower detection rates in dogs (Finelli et al., 2000).

In humans, vegetation complexity could impede a clear view of the carcasses (Borner et al., 2017; Eckstein, 2011). To characterize the vegetation in each search plot, we measured six variables related to vegetation height and cover (Table 1) in four non-overlapping circular areas of 5-m radius. The location of the centre of these areas was defined randomly using a random point generator (Beyer, 2004). For each measured variable, we took the average value of the four areas and used it as a covariate in the analysis.

Weather conditions are likely to affect searcher motivation and fatigue, as well as odour production and dispersion (Dahlgren et al., 2011). For this analysis, we used the daily mean wind speed (km/hr) and mean temperature (°C) for the Masegoso municipality (1 km away from the nearest wind turbine), obtained from the meteorological web site www.eltie mpo.es.

## **2.4** | **Data analysis**

To study the performance of dogs and humans we defined a binary variable (1; detection, 0; non-detection) and modelled the probability of carcass detection (p) using generalized linear mixed models (GLMM). We applied a logit link to the mean response (p) and defined a Bernoulli error structure. Thus, the search of each individual carcass is considered one trial and the GLMMs modelled the log-odds of detection, defining odds as the ratio between the probability of detecting and the probability of missing a carcass. We used a hypothesis-driven approach (Burnham & Anderson, 2001), testing different combinations of fixed and random effects based on plausible hypothesis and ranking them by their predictive ability, based on leave-one-out cross validation (LOO; Hooten & Hobbs, 2015; Vehtari, Gelman, & Gabry, 2017). All numerical variables were centred and scaled to twice their standard deviations (Gelman, 2008). Models were fitted to data in a Bayesian framework, using the software _JAGS_ (Plummer, 2003) to implement Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling. We ran the analysis in r (R Core Team, 2018), using the package jagsUI (Kellner, 2018) and the package loo (Vehtari, Gabry, Yao, & Gelman, 2018) to calculate a leave-one-out cross validation information criterion (LOOIC, lower values represent better predictive power). We specified normally distributed priors, with mean 0 and variance 1, for the regression coefficients and ran three chains of 10,000 iterations, discarding the first 5,000.

Models tested whether variables related to weather, vegetation or characteristics of the carcass, influenced detection probability and to what degree. To formally perform tests on differing effects for dogs and humans, all models included an indicator variable for the type of searcher (Table 2), as well as its interactions with all the other covariates (Table 3). To reduce the dimensionality of the vegetation descriptors and to prevent multicollinearity in the models (Quinn & Keough, 2002), we performed a principal component analysis (PCA) using the software STATISTICA 7 (StatSoft Inc., 2011) and we used the varimax-rotated factor loadings as covariates in the GLMMs, in place of the original vegetation variables.

**TA B LE 2** Variables used in models. The _values_ column shows the levels of the categorical variables and the range of the numerical ones

**TA B LE 3** Models fitted to detection data and corresponding leave-one-out cross validation (LOOIC) scores. The hypothesis column refers to the variables considered affecting the probability of detection under each model. The fixed effects are specified using: ‘+’ additive effect and ‘*’ interaction effect. All models consider a random intercept term to account for differences between search days, with the exception of the last two, which incorporate random effects for turbine ( _t_ ) and individual searcher ( _i_ ), respectively

We tested random intercepts for the variables ID, DATE and TURB, to account for the influence of particular characteristics of the individual searcher, uncontrolled conditions in the day of search and characteristics of the search plot, other than vegetation structure, respectively (Table 3). We tested the random effects in the full model (GLMM7) using LOOIC scores, keeping only those that improved the predictive performance of the model with no random effects. We used those same random effects in simpler models (i.e. all models kept the same set of random effects). Random intercepts were given normal priors, with mean 0 and variance uniformly distributed between 0 and 1.

## **3** | **RESULTS**

We used the first three principal components obtained in the PCA analysis, which accounted for 72.3% of the observed variance in vegetation variables (Table 1). The first component (PC1, 26.8% of variance explained) describes a gradient in shrub development related to cover of medium to tall evergreen shrub formations (30 cm to 3 m high). The second component (PC2, 26% of explained variance) differentiates open plots dominated by grassland (<10 cm high) with few trees (>3 m high) from those with abundant trees and little grass. Finally, the third component (PC3, 19.6% of variance explained) separates plots with larger portions of bare ground.

Overall, dogs detected 77.3% of the total number of carcasses ( _n_ = 589), while humans only detected 21.5% ( _n_ = 121). According to the LOOIC scores, we found no evidence of improved predictions by including random variation in detection probability either across wind turbines or individual searchers. However, we found support for random variation in detection probability across search days (Table 3). Thus, all models were fitted with random intercepts for dates (DATE) as a random effect.

Models GLMM1 and GLMM4 were ranked as the best predictive configurations with similar LOOIC scores (<1% difference, Table 3). A post-hoc comparison showed that a model including vegetation was better at predicting probability of detection if only human detection trials were analysed ( _c_ . 3.5% reduction in LOOIC), but not if only dog detection trials were considered ( _c_ . 1% increase in LOOIC). Therefore, GLMM4 was favoured, since it incorporates vegetation variables that are relevant for one type of searcher (see Section 4: Discussion).

According to GLMM4, human searchers are strongly affected by the size of the carcass compared to dogs, as reflected by a positive interaction effect between TYPE and SIZE (Table 4). The model estimates a positive, although weak, average effect of wingspan on dog's detection odds of between 0% and 2.3% for a 1 cm increase in wingspan (95% credible interval), while this effect is on average 1%–6% for humans. The uncertainty around the estimated effect increases for the largest wingspans analysed due to a lower proportion of this type of carcass in our samples (Figure 2).

Odds of detection using dogs are mostly unaffected by changing vegetation structure (no effect of PC1, PC2 or PC3; Figure 2), while there is compelling evidence of a negative interaction effect between PC1 and type of searcher (Table 2). This means that detection odds tend to decline faster for humans than for dogs as PC1 (cover of medium to tall vegetation) increases. A 95% credible interval for the effect of PC1 on the probability of detection in humans ranges from −70% to +20%. Most of the posterior distribution is negative, suggesting lower probability of detection in humans as PC1 increases.

The average wind speed during the trials was 20.16 km/hr ( _SD_ = 8.14 km/hr) and the average temperature 13.54°C ( _SD_ = 8.84°C). The inclusion of weather variables did not improve the predictive power of the model. However, we detected random variation in searcher performance associated with the date of search. weather conditions throughout the day, we tested whether the order in which searchers were conducted had an effect on detection probability. To do this, we included order of search in GLMM4 and compared this model with the original one (without order as an explanatory variable) using their LOOIC scores. A slight increase of <0.1% on the LOOIC score when including order in the model (irrespective of the type of searcher), suggests that this variable does not improve model predictions, and therefore we favoured the simpler model.

## **4** | **DISCUSSION**

Most studies to date analyse detection performance from an experimental setting, using carcasses of only a few species, covering a narrow range of environmental conditions or from a meta-analysis perspective (Arnett, 2006; Mathews et al., 2013; Paula et al., 2011; Reyes et al., 2016, for experimental designs and Barrientos et al., 2018; Smallwood, 2007 for meta-analyses). Our work provides a direct comparison of how variables affected dogs and humans empirically

within the same study, using a single search protocol, which allowed us to reduce the effect of uncontrolled variables and compare covariates more clearly (see Smallwood et al., 2020, for a similar approach). We conducted detection trials in different weather, involving a large number of carcasses of various sizes, and characterizing the vegetation at the search areas in detail. This design facilitated ranking variables by their influence on detection rates.

Our results confirmed that dogs are two- to three-fold more efficient than human searchers at detecting bird and bat carcasses, and size of the target was the most important variable for detection, once type of searcher was accounted for. We also confirmed that detection rates fell steeply for humans as target size decreased, while dogs suffered only a small reduction in their effectiveness, retaining high success rates throughout the analysed wingspan range. Although some authors suggest that differences in detection probability among different carcass sizes could be caused by small carcasses being scavenged quicker than large ones (Smallwood, 2007), our data show that even with no scavenging, small carcasses are less likely to be detected by humans. Our estimates of dog's detection performance may have been influenced by having a member of the search team placing carcasses for the dogs (Lit, Schweitzer, & Oberbauer, 2011). However, our handlers followed a fixed search pattern and minimized the instructions given to the dogs during the search, and consequently, the influence of the handler in the dog's work. Still, we consider that conducting blind searches is preferable to avoid potential biases and also to test dog and handler as a team. Another potential source of bias was humans conducting fewer trials than dogs, which could have given the latter extra practice. However, in this case, we discard practice being a significant advantage since all searchers were previously experienced on carcass searching. We observed that vegetation structure did not affect dog's performance, but it influenced human searchers. Humans being particularly challenged in dense bush areas, supports our hypothesis that this type of vegetation blocks searcher vision and restricts searcher access to the target. On the contrary, dog's performance was unaffected by vegetation structure, suggesting little effect on scent dispersion. However, we agree with the suggestion by Paula et al. (2011) in that certain types of habitats may be inaccessible also for dogs, particularly if they work on a leash (see Mathews et al., 2013), which may explain the negative effect of vegetation on dog performance observed in other studies (Arnett, 2006; Mathews et al., 2013). Some authors previously concluded that habitat complexity reduced the performance of humans or dogs (Arnett, 2006; Mathews et al., 2013; Smallwood, 2007), while others found that habitat was unimportant for carcass detection (Barrientos et al., 2018; Paula et al., 2011). Based on our analysis, we believe that a small effect of habitat on detection probabilities compared to other variables, such as target size, or notably, type of searcher, can lead to model selection procedures penalizing the inclusion of habitat variables if dogs and humans are analysed together. However, the predictive accuracy of the models considering only humans improves when vegetation characteristics are accounted for. Furthermore, differences in human detection probabilities observed across studies may be partly

explained by the effect of vegetation. For example, considering the reference habitat in our study area (relatively dense bush), our model predicts the probability of a human detecting a carcass of the smallest size ( _c_ . 0 g) being around 10%. This figure agrees with Stevens, Reese, and Connelly (2011) and Mathews et al. (2013), who worked on closed habitats, but it is lower than suggested by other studies conducted in open vegetation (14%–40%, see Arnett, 2006; Reyes et al., 2016). However, detection probabilities for the smallest targets predicted by our model increases to 28%, if we set vegetation to be open with abundant bare ground, which agrees better with other authors working in open habitats. Further disagreement in probability of detection between studies may be attributed to particularities of habitats and protocols used for the searches.

Daily average wind speed and temperature did not have a systematic effect on searcher's efficiency. We did not observe systematic variation in probability of detection throughout the day either, which reinforces our perception of weather conditions being unimportant for searcher efficiency. Although the search protocol—designed to search on days without precipitation or strong winds—could have biased the data towards mild weather conditions (see Table 2), our results are consistent with those observed in other studies (Barrientos et al., 2018; Leigh & Dominick, 2015; Paula et al., 2011; Reed, Bidlack, Hurt, & Getz, 2011). Nevertheless, we found random variation in detection rates on different days, which could be capturing the effect of unmeasured weather conditions, as well as other factors, such as searcher focus, motivation and fatigue. While other variables associated with weather, such as relative humidity and barometric pressure could influence searcher's detection performance, they are correlated with temperature and wind speed (e.g. Lawrence, 2005), and therefore, we believe they would not explain variation in detection probability any further. However, we consider that measuring weather variables at the exact time and location of the search (as opposed to using daily averages), could provide additional insights on their effect on detection probability (Fogarty, Elmore, Fuhlendorf, & Loss, 2018).

From the logistics standpoint, we found that, by using external technicians with their own dogs, many challenges attributed to the use of dogs, including their care, maintenance and training, could be circumvented. Although the service cost of dog handlers was approximately 40% higher than that of human searchers, the improved results compensated for the extra expenditure (also see Smallwood et al., 2020). Therefore, the question to be posed is whether this extra precision provided by dogs aids conservation efforts and should be a requirement by management agencies and for research projects.

## **5** | **CONCLUSIONS**

Our study underlines the good performance of search dogs under a variety of conditions and target sizes, which makes them valuable and cost-effective when extra precision is required. Like previous authors, we recommend the use of dogs to avoid biasing detection rates towards large targets. We also recommend using dogs in areas of dense vegetation, based on their consistently high performance

in different habitats. Humans on the contrary would need a more thorough search protocol to cover dense vegetation effectively, at the cost of increased search time. We support the establishment of clearly defined search patterns to homogenize the coverage of the search area, and to facilitate comparison across studies and searchers. Nevertheless, we favour search protocols that allow dogs to move freely within search bands (i.e. without a leash), to minimize accessibility restrictions imposed by the handler, at least when working in dense vegetation. Full coverage of the search area is not always possible, which may have an impact on searcher efficiency. In this sense, we recommend mapping locations that are inaccessible for the searchers and further study how accessibility influences searcher efficiency. Tracking devices attached to the searchers (e.g. GPS) may prove useful to this end.
